newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: FEATURE - Zimbabwe's Mugabe under fire as hardships grow.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Zimbabwe's Mugabe under fire as hardships grow.

text.p: Zimbabwe's President Robert Mugabe is coming under stinging criticism over his personal life at a time when he is asking his people to tighten their belts and help pull the economy out of the doldrums.

Mugabe, a 72-year-old ex-guerrilla who has led the country since independence from Britain in 1980, kept his family life out of public scrutiny until he married his former secretary, 31-year-old Grace Marufu, at a lavish wedding in August.

Now frustration at mounting economic hardship and accusations of mismanagement in a country that has struggled to boost growth above one percent annually for the past five years have turned the spotlight on the president himself.
Over the past few months, independent newspapers have been filled with unusually sharp criticism of what writers see as the First Family's spendthrift ways.
Most complaints are directed at Mugabe's frequent trips outside the country, which have earned him the nickname Vasco da Gama after the Portuguese explorer.
In the past 10 months, he and his wife have been on 31 trips abroad and he has not responded to the rising criticism.
Officials of the beleaguered airline Air Zimbabwe say that each time he travels, flights are further disrupted because it is left short of planes.

The airline, which often apologises for delayed flights due to plane shortages, has become the butt of cynical jokes, some rewriting its corporate slogan -- "A Commitment to Excellency" -- as "A Commitment to His Excellency".
"THE VISITING PRESIDENT"

"The citizens of Zimbabwe have begun to call our president 'the Visiting President'. He visits us every now and then, departs for some unknown destination, unknown cause, and at the same time leaves the national house burning down," wrote prominent author and political commentator Chenjerai Hove.
"Nigerian novelist Chinua Achebe once wrote about 'the problem with Nigeria'. We might as well write the problem with Zimbabwe...an arrogant leadership which always thinks this country is a prison."

Hove was writing in the Zimbabwe Independent after Mugabe flew to a food summit in Italy, leaving about 10,000 nurses and doctors on the streets in a month-long strike for higher pay that paralysed government hospitals.

The strike followed a wider stoppage by most of the country's 180,000 civil servants in August, during which demonstrators angrily accused Mugabe of insensitivity for hosting a huge wedding a week earlier while telling them his government had no money to pay them higher salaries.
"Mugabe: We want more money so that we can also wed in the same way as you did with Grace," read a protest placard.

One reader, in a letter to the Zimbabwe Independent, said he saw nothing extraordinary about press reports lambasting Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko's extravagant lifestyle abroad while his country was falling apart at the seams.
"To a more or lesser extent, every African president has the same lifestyle. We don't have to look any further than our own doorstep to prove this."
30-ROOM MANSION FOR WIFE

The First Family has also drawn fire following allegations in the independent media that the cash-strapped government diverted money for housing for low-to-medium-income earners to build a Z$6 million (US$558,000), 30-room mansion for Grace in a posh Harare suburb.
Government officials have declined comment, saying the issue is a family matter.

"Not so long ago there were numerous pronouncements from the political leadership calling for the people to 'tighten their belts' in the face of economic reforms," says political commentator Lupi Mushayakarara.

"In spite of the irony of asking those already existing on a porridge and matemba (dried fish) diet to further emaciate themselves, one understood the benefits of sacrificing the present conveniences for future gains.

"But given recent exposes about the shameless extravagance of the First Family, it is safer perhaps to conclude that the leadership has now abandoned the austerity process in favour of a dog-eat-dog culture," she said.
($1=10.755 Zimbabwe dollars)
